# A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration: Nine-Month Results

*Varden County Evaluation Unit, in collaboration with the Department of Labour Economics, Easterly University. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony and D. Rao. Registered protocol VC-2023-04.*

## Summary

We randomly assigned 24 administrative offices of a county government, employing 1,180 staff, to either reduce scheduled hours from 37.5 to 30 per week at full pay (12 offices) or continue on the standard schedule (12 offices) for nine months. Output was measured from administrative records, not from manager assessments, and actual hours from timesheets. The effect differed sharply by type of work. In case-processing offices, where work arrives as a backlog that can be cleared at any time, output per full-time employee changed by −2.1% (95% CI −6.8 to +2.6) relative to control and output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. In counter and contact-centre offices, where output depends on staff being present while the public is waiting, output per employee fell by 11.4% (95% CI −16.9 to −5.9), waiting times rose, and output per actual hour rose by a more modest 6.7%. Sick days fell by 29% across treated offices. An exploratory analysis suggests that a reduction in recurring meetings may account for part of the gain in case-processing offices.

## Motivation

Existing evidence on reduced working time comes mainly from voluntary pilots without comparison groups, in which output is often reported by the managers who sponsored the change. The county wished to know whether a reduced schedule could be extended to its own administrative staff without loss of service, and agreed to a randomised design with administrative output measures and a registered analysis plan.

## Design

**Units and randomisation.** The 24 offices were stratified into two strata by type of work before randomisation, and offices were randomised within strata:

- *Case-processing offices* (14 offices; 7 treated, 7 control): permits, licensing, benefits assessment and records. Work arrives as cases that join a queue and can be completed at any point within statutory deadlines.
- *Counter and contact-centre offices* (10 offices; 5 treated, 5 control): in-person service counters and telephone lines. Work arrives as members of the public who must be served while they wait.

Randomisation was at office level to avoid contamination between colleagues. Treated offices kept their public opening hours unchanged; staff rotas were rearranged so that each employee worked 30 scheduled hours.

**Outcomes.** The registered primary outcome is output per full-time-equivalent employee (FTE), measured as cases closed (case-processing) or contacts handled (counter and contact centre), from the county's case-management and telephony systems. Registered secondary outcomes are output per actual hour (from timesheets, which include any overtime claimed), quality (the share of decisions overturned on appeal; for contact centres, the repeat-contact rate within seven days), average waiting time, and sick days. Analysis is difference-in-differences against the six-month pre-period, with standard errors clustered by office.

**Exploratory measures.** At the request of office managers we also collected calendar data on recurring meetings in month six. This was not part of the registered plan.

## Results

### Hours

Scheduled hours fell by 20% in treated offices. Actual hours, from timesheets, fell by less: by 13% in case-processing offices (from 37.9 to 33.0 per week) and by 17% in counter offices (from 37.6 to 31.2), the difference reflecting overtime claimed to clear backlogs in case-processing. Control offices' actual hours were stable.

### Output and quality

**Table 1. Difference-in-differences estimates at nine months, treated relative to control**

| Outcome | Case-processing (7 v 7 offices) | Counter and contact centre (5 v 5 offices) |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −11.4% (−16.9 to −5.9) |
| Actual hours per FTE | −13% | −17% |
| Output per actual hour | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +6.7% (+0.4 to +13.3) |
| Appeal overturn rate / repeat contact rate | 3.1% v 3.0% | 11.8% v 10.9% |
| Average wait (minutes), treated offices, pre → month 9 | — | 4.2 → 6.9 |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% (both strata pooled) | |

In case-processing offices, output per employee was statistically indistinguishable from control, with a point estimate slightly below zero, and quality was unchanged. Because actual hours fell by 13%, output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. Measured against scheduled rather than actual hours, the gain would appear as 22%; we regard that figure as misleading, because staff did not in fact work only the scheduled hours.

In counter and contact-centre offices, the picture is different. With the same number of staff each working fewer hours, fewer staff were present at any given time during unchanged opening hours. Contacts handled per employee fell by 11.4% and the average wait rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes. Output per actual hour rose by 6.7%, but this did not offset the loss of hours, and the service the public received was worse. Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10% of calls.

### Wellbeing

Sick days fell by 29% in treated offices relative to control. Resignations were lower in treated offices (annualised 3.9% against 7.4%), though with 12 offices per arm and few resignations the estimate is imprecise.

### Exploratory: meetings

Calendar data in month six showed that staff in treated case-processing offices spent 3.8 hours per week in recurring meetings against 7.1 hours in control case-processing offices, a difference of 3.3 hours. Offices that cut meetings most showed the largest gains in output per hour (correlation across the 7 treated offices, r = 0.71). Interviews suggested that the reduced schedule prompted managers to cancel standing meetings that had persisted by habit.

We emphasise that this analysis was not registered, that it rests on seven offices, and that a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism. We report it because, if confirmed, it would mean that a substantial part of the per-hour gain comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest alone, and that would matter for how the result is interpreted and for what other employers could expect. We have registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up.

## Discussion

Three conclusions follow from the registered analyses.

First, in work where output is not tied to presence, a 20% cut in scheduled hours produced a much smaller cut in actual hours and little or no measurable loss of output per employee. Output per hour rose by about an eighth.

Second, in work where output is tied to presence, the same change reduced output per employee by about a tenth and worsened service, even though each hour worked was somewhat more productive. Gains per hour do not by themselves imply that the hours reduction pays for itself. The question "does a shorter week raise productivity?" therefore has at least two answers depending on whether productivity is understood per hour or per employee, and these come apart most sharply in coverage-bound work.

Third, estimates computed against scheduled hours materially overstate the per-hour gain. In our data the overstatement is from 12.5% to 22% in case-processing offices.

These findings qualify claims, made on the basis of uncontrolled pilots, that reduced hours are sector-general. A sector may contain both kinds of work; what matters is whether output in a given role depends on hours of presence.

## Limitations

The trial is in one public employer, with 24 offices; confidence intervals are correspondingly wide, particularly in the counter stratum. Staff knew their assignment, and control staff knew that a trial was under way, which could have affected effort in either direction. Nine months may be too short to reveal whether gains persist after the novelty of the change wears off, or whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines. Public-sector case processing may differ from private-sector knowledge work in ways that affect the result. A 24-month follow-up is under way.

response:
# Review of the Varden County 30-Hour Week Trial

This is a much stronger study than the Halden pilot. It fixes most of the problems I raised there:

- **A comparison group**, randomised within strata.
- **Output from administrative records**, not manager judgement.
- **Actual hours from timesheets**, not scheduled hours.
- **A registered primary outcome**, with clustered standard errors.
- **Exploratory work clearly labelled** as unregistered.

The authors also refuse to report the inflated scheduled-hours figure as their headline, and their caveats on the meetings analysis are appropriately cautious.

I checked the arithmetic and it holds:

| Figure | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Case-processing, output per actual hour | 0.979 / 0.87 | +12.5% |
| Case-processing, against scheduled hours | 0.979 / 0.80 | +22.4% |
| Counter, output per actual hour | 0.886 / 0.83 | +6.7% |
| Case-processing hours | 37.9 → 33.0 | −12.9% |
| Counter hours | 37.6 → 31.2 | −17.0% |

The per-hour confidence intervals are also consistent with the per-FTE ones. The remaining issues are about interpretation and reporting, not basic validity.

## 1. Demand may have shifted between treated and control offices

Randomising by office prevents contamination between colleagues. It does not prevent the *work* moving between offices, and both strata are exposed to that.

**Counter and contact centres.** The 11.4% fall in contacts handled is larger than the abandonment figures can explain. Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10%, so the share of calls answered fell by about 4%. The rest of the gap could come from:

- members of the public going to other offices or channels;
- calls being rerouted to other lines;
- people being deterred from making contact at all.

If some of that demand went to *control* offices, control output rose as treated output fell. The difference-in-differences estimate would then exaggerate the harm.

**Case-processing.** Cases closed depends on cases received. If cases are drawn from a county-wide queue, or reallocated when an office falls behind, treated offices may have received fewer cases. That would hide a real loss of capacity.

The paper should state how demand reaches each office. It should also report cases and contacts *received* by arm, not just those handled.

## 2. Ten clusters are too few for standard clustered standard errors

The counter stratum has 5 offices per arm, and the case-processing stratum 7 per arm. Conventional cluster-robust standard errors are known to be too small with this few clusters. The intervals in Table 1, especially for the counter stratum, may be too narrow.

The authors should report wild-cluster bootstrap or randomisation-inference p-values. A randomised design makes the latter natural.

They should also:

- **Test the difference between strata formally.** "Differed sharply by type of work" is the headline claim, but no interaction test is reported. A rough calculation from the reported intervals suggests the difference (about 9 points) is likely significant, but that should be shown.
- **Say whether the stratum-specific analysis was pre-registered** as a primary comparison or added later. The registered primary outcome is output per FTE, yet no pooled estimate is reported.

## 3. Higher output per hour at counters may just mean busier staff

When the same public demand meets fewer staff, each staff member spends less time idle between contacts. Output per hour rises because the queue is longer, not because people are working more efficiently. Longer waits and more abandoned calls are exactly what you would see.

So "each hour worked was somewhat more productive" (Discussion) is at least partly the other side of worse service. It should not be read as an efficiency gain that could be harvested elsewhere.

A related point: repeat contacts rose from 10.9% to 11.8%. If repeat calls count as handled contacts, they inflate output. The text does not mention this quality result at all.

## 4. Case-processing output could hide backlog growth and cream-skimming

**Backlog and time to decision.** Nearly flat cases closed is compatible with a growing backlog or longer processing times, which the Limitations acknowledge. Backlog size, case age and the share of cases decided within statutory deadlines should be reported. All three are available from the same case-management system.

**Case mix.** An unweighted count of cases closed rewards closing easy cases first. A breakdown by case type or complexity would address this.

**Appeal overturn rates lag.** Decisions made in months 7 to 9 will mostly not have reached appeal by month 9. "Quality unchanged" is premature, and should be revisited at 24 months.

## 5. Inconsistencies in Table 1

- **Mixed estimates.** The table is titled "difference-in-differences estimates", but several rows are not:
  - quality is shown as two levels (3.1% v 3.0%; 11.8% v 10.9%), with no confidence interval;
  - waiting time is shown for treated offices only, before and after, with no control comparison;
  - sick days are pooled across strata, with no confidence interval.
- **Missing results.** Abandoned calls (6% → 10%) appear only in the text, again treated-only. All secondary outcomes should be estimated the same way as the primary one, with intervals.
- **Hours explanation.** Actual hours fell less than scheduled hours in *both* strata: counter staff averaged 31.2 hours against 30 scheduled. The text attributes the gap only to backlog overtime in case-processing, so it should account for the counter overtime too.

## 6. Two definitions need tightening

**FTE.** The paper uses "per FTE" and "per employee" interchangeably. If a 30-hour contract counted as 0.8 FTE, per-FTE output would be a different quantity. The paper should state that FTE is fixed at the pre-trial contracted headcount.

**The form of the 30-hour week.**
- If it was a four-day week, part of the 29% fall in sick days is mechanical: there are fewer working days on which to be absent.
- If it was five shorter days, there is no such effect.
- The paper should say which, and report sick days per scheduled day.

**Timesheets.** Timesheets capture overtime that is *claimed*. Unclaimed work, such as salaried staff finishing cases at home, would make actual hours look lower than they were and the per-hour gain look larger. This is the same bias the authors rightly criticise in scheduled-hours estimates, on a smaller scale.

## 7. The meetings analysis says more than the authors claim, and less

**Less.** With 7 offices, r = 0.71 has a 95% confidence interval of roughly −0.09 to 0.95 (p ≈ 0.07). It is not distinguishable from zero. The authors' caveats are appropriate, but the number should be stated. The comparison is also a single cross-section at month 6 with no pre-period meeting data. The 3.3-hour gap assumes the arms started out similar, which randomising 7 offices per arm does not guarantee.

**More.** If meeting time is counted in timesheet hours, the numbers suggest that most of the hours reduction came out of meetings:

| | Actual hours | Meetings | Hours outside meetings |
|---|---|---|---|
| Control | ~37.9 | 7.1 | ~30.8 |
| Treated | 33.0 | 3.8 | 29.2 |

Non-meeting time was about 5% lower in treated offices, against a 2.1% fall in output. That implies a gain per non-meeting hour of only about 3%. This rests on the assumptions above, but if it holds, most of the 12.5% "productivity gain" is fewer meetings rather than more effective working time.

That supports the authors' hypothesis more strongly than the correlation does. It also suggests a cheaper intervention, cutting meetings without cutting hours, which the 24-month follow-up could test directly.

## 8. Smaller points

- **The counter result is partly built into the design.** Fixed opening hours, fixed headcount and fewer hours per person must mean fewer staff on duty at any moment. The more informative question is the cost of keeping service levels the same, for example the extra staff needed. A short costing would make this finding much more useful to the county.
- **Awareness of the trial.** Control staff knowing a trial was under way could cause rivalry (working harder) or demoralisation (working less), and these would push the estimates in opposite directions. Any survey or engagement data from control offices would help.
- **Resignations** are reported as levels (3.9% v 7.4%) without a pre-period baseline or interval. They should be treated like the other outcomes, or dropped from the Summary.

## Overall

The main conclusions are well supported:

- per-hour and per-employee productivity diverge;
- coverage-bound work behaves differently from backlog work;
- scheduled-hours denominators overstate gains.

The Discussion is appropriately restrained. The changes I would prioritise before publication are:

1. Address demand displacement between arms (point 1).
2. Use small-cluster inference and a formal test between strata (point 2).
3. Estimate all secondary outcomes as difference-in-differences with intervals, and add backlog and case-age measures (points 4–5).
4. Clarify the FTE definition and the form of the 30-hour week (point 6).
